The presidential candidate of the Young Progressives Party, Peter Agada, has condemned the attacks on the convoys of the Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and his running mate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, warning that the growing political violence could discourage Nigerians, particularly professionals, from participating in the democratic process. Agada said attacks on political convoys, destruction of campaign banners and billboards, and clashes among supporters of rival political groups were creating an increasingly hostile political atmosphere ahead of the 2027 general elections. The YPP candidate, who spoke on Tuesday at the unveiling of his manifesto in Abuja, said many professionals who could contribute meaningfully to national development were withdrawing from the political space because of the violence and hostility among political actors. He said, “A good number of Nigerian professionals seem to be stepping back and folding their arms to watch the violence going on right now in the political scene. It is increasingly becoming very unpalatable to watch the fights and violence between all the different juggernauts and attacks on these convoys. “Sometimes, opposition campaign banners and billboards are pulled down and vandalised. This situation is giving Nigerians and people who really love this country a lot of concern.” His condemnation comes amid recent attacks on opposition politicians and their supporters in different parts of the country. A few days ago, the convoy of Kwankwaso, the NDC vice-presidential candidate, and the party’s Kano State governorship candidate, Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo, was attacked by suspected political thugs in Bichi Local Government Area of Kano State. Similarly, the convoy of Obi and some NDC supporters reportedly came under attack in Calabar, Cross River State, shortly after the former Anambra State governor arrived in the state capital for the party’s presidential town hall meeting at Metropolitan Hotel. The attacks have heightened concerns over political intolerance and the safety of candidates and their supporters as parties intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 elections. The Senate also raised concerns over electoral violence on Tuesday, urging the Independent National Electoral Commission to disqualify any political candidate whose supporters were found to have instigated or participated in violence, subject to established court convictions and the provisions of the 2026 Electoral Act. The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, backed the position, calling on INEC to ensure strict enforcement of the law irrespective of political affiliation. “Any candidate or supporter caught instigating violence, INEC has the right to disqualify them. We should call the attention of INEC to the 2026 Electoral Act; no matter the political party, such a candidate should immediately be disqualified. They are embedded in the 2026 Electoral Act and require strong implementation,” he said. Meanwhile, Agada, while expressing concern over the political atmosphere, said he remained open to working with other opposition leaders to address the country’s challenges but insisted that any coalition must be based on a shared policy framework. He spoke amid speculation that he might withdraw from the presidential race to support President Bola Tinubu or another opposition candidate, including Atiku Abubakar and Obi. The YPP candidate said the question of stepping down had not arisen, adding that his immediate priority was to present his Labour Direct manifesto to Nigerians. He, however, said he would be willing to engage other political leaders whose policy documents and development proposals aligned with his agenda. “If we see persons with a framework, policy document and architecture that resembles what we are talking about today, and I see those numbers aligning with what I just read, I’m going to connect with them, and we’re going to give this a fight until Nigeria changes and aligns,” he said. Agada argued that the country needed collective leadership rather than an arrangement centred on one individual, adding that whoever emerged as the leader of a possible coalition would matter less than agreement on its governing principles. “In the military rank and file, it is the man with the vision who calls the numbers and delineates the pathway accurately who should lead. Once we align, whoever takes the leadership doesn’t really matter then. I believe that we can all work together and tackle Nigeria from different sides,” he said. He added that Nigeria’s challenges were too complex to be resolved by one individual, insisting that the country needed people with different expertise and ideas to work together. “We are in a dire strait. The country does not need just one man. We need many people looking at Nigeria’s challenges and trying to solve the problem. It’s not a one-man thing. Nigeria’s problem is complex; hence we need good minds working together,” Agada said.
